specPoints.text: understand the meaning of the term codominance

primer.text: Codominance breaks the habit of one allele bossing the other. This note shows what happens when both members of a genotype are expressed, using the ABO blood groups, three alleles strong, as the classic case, and then walks a genetic diagram that predicts when two ordinary parents can surprise everyone with a group O child.

lessons.title: Both Alleles Expressed
lessons.opening: Codominance breaks the usual dominant-versus-recessive pattern: when the two alleles of a genotype are both expressed, the phenotype shows the contribution of each, and the ABO blood groups supply the classic illustration with three alleles instead of two.
keyPoints: Codominance means both alleles of a genotype show their effect in the organism's traits.
The ABO gene carries three alleles, written with superscripts A, B and O.
Allele IA yields antigen A, allele IB yields antigen B, and allele IO yields no antigens.
IA and IB are codominant with each other, and both are dominant over IO.

low.restatement: Neither allele hides the other; both leave their mark on the observable characteristic.
low.analogy: Two authors who both sign the book, rather than one editor overwriting the other.
low.examPointer: Learn the antigen map: IA gives A, IB gives B, IO gives neither.

medium.restatement: Three alleles expand the genotype menu beyond the usual two-version gene, so phenotype combinations multiply.
medium.analogy: A dial with three settings instead of a simple on-off switch.
medium.examPointer: State the dominance order precisely: codominance between IA and IB, both dominant to IO.

check.stem: What does codominance mean for the two alleles in a genotype?

options.text: Both are expressed in the phenotype
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The stronger one masks the weaker
options.explanation: Masking describes dominance, the pattern codominance replaces.

options.text: They blend into an intermediate average
options.explanation: Blending is a common misconception; both products appear instead.
Cancellation would leave no expression at all.

check.stem: How many alleles does the ABO blood group gene have?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Two is the usual count; this gene carries three.
No fourth allele exists in the taught system.
That number belongs to chromosome pairs, not alleles here.

check.stem: Which allele produces no antigens on the blood cells?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
That allele produces antigen A.
That allele produces antigen B.
IO produces none, which is why group O exists.

check.stem: What is the relationship between IA and IB, given that they are codominant?

options.text: They are codominant with each other
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Neither masks the other; both are expressed.
The taught order is codominance, not one-way dominance.
Both are dominant to IO, the reverse.

check.stem: Which statement about the O blood group is right?

options.text: A person with genotype IOIO makes no A or B antigens
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Group O carries antigen A quietly
options.explanation: Antigen A requires the IA allele.
Both antigens require IA and IB together.

options.text: Group O depends on a fourth allele
options.explanation: Only the three taught alleles exist.

check.stem: Name the antigen produced by each of the three ABO alleles.
check.modelAnswer: IA produces antigen A, IB produces antigen B, and IO produces no antigens.
Codominance describes a genotype whose two alleles each leave a visible mark on the organism's traits.

check.stem: Explain why a child of group O can be born to a group A parent and a group B parent.
check.modelAnswer: Each parent can carry the IO allele alongside their main allele, so the child can inherit IO from both and, with no antigen A or antigen B made, belongs to group O.

check.stem: A blood-group A parent and a blood-group B parent have a group O child. What genotypes must the parents carry, and what chance does another child have of group O?
check.modelAnswer: Each parent is heterozygous, carrying IO with their codominant partner allele, so each pregnancy has a one-in-four, or 25 percent, chance of a group O child.

lessons.title: Reading the Codominance Diagram
lessons.opening: Genetic diagrams handle codominance exactly like any other cross: write the parental genotypes, split the alleles around the square, and read the offspring combinations, keeping in mind that heterozygous A and B parents can each hand on the O allele.
keyPoints: Parental genotypes are written first, then alleles are placed around the square.
A group A parent in this example carries IAIO, and the group B parent carries IBIO.
An O child proves each parent handed on an IO allele.
Parents of these types have a one-in-four chance of another group O child.

low.restatement: The square pairs one allele from each parent in every cell, giving four combinations.
low.analogy: A menu where you pick one item from each of two columns and every pairing is a possible meal.
low.examPointer: Say one-in-four, or 25 percent, whenever the O outcome is asked as a chance.

medium.restatement: Each parent produces two gamete types, IA and IO or IB and IO, so the grid fills with four pairings.
medium.analogy: Two coin tosses at once: the four faces of the square mirror the four pairings.
medium.examPointer: Quote gamete types, not phenotype guesses, when justifying the square.

check.stem: In the worked diagram, why must the group A parent be IAIO rather than IAIA?

options.text: Only a hidden IO allele lets a group O child be produced
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: IAIA would weaken the parent's blood
options.explanation: Homozygous IA has no such effect.

options.text: The diagram needs a shorter label
options.explanation: Genotypes are chosen by genetics, not typography.

options.text: Group A cannot exist with two alleles
options.explanation: Group A commonly appears as either IAIA or IAIO.

check.stem: What fraction of the offspring from IAIO crossed with IBIO is expected to be group O?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Only one of the four cells gives IOIO.
Three cells produce groups A, B or AB instead.
The IOIO cell exists whenever both parents carry IO.

check.stem: Which offspring genotype carries both antigen A and antigen B?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
That genotype produces antigen A only.
That genotype produces antigen B only.
That genotype produces no antigens at all.

check.stem: What does the diagram assume about how the two parents' alleles combine?

options.text: Each gamete carries one allele, and fertilisation pairs them at random
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Gametes hold one allele of each gene.

options.text: Alleles are chosen to fit the phenotype
options.explanation: The pairing is random, not chosen.
Every allele, including IO, appears in gametes.

check.stem: A group AB child is produced from this cross. Which parent contributed what?

options.text: The A parent gave IA and the B parent gave IB
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
IOIO offspring are group O, not AB.

options.text: The O allele produced the AB group
options.explanation: IO produces no antigen, so it cannot create AB.

options.text: Both alleles came from the mother
options.explanation: Each parent contributes one allele of the pair.

check.stem: List the four offspring genotypes shown by the IAIO by IBIO square.
check.modelAnswer: The combinations are IAIB, IAIO, IBIO and IOIO, each occupying one cell of the diagram.

check.stem: State the probability that this particular cross yields a group O child.
check.modelAnswer: The chance is one cell out of four, so 25 percent.

check.stem: Explain why knowing a child's blood group can reveal hidden parental genotypes.
check.modelAnswer: A group O child must have received an IO allele from each parent, so each parent must carry IO even if their own phenotype is A or B.

check.stem: Two parents, both IAIO, plan a family. Predict the possible offspring blood groups and the chance of group O.
check.modelAnswer: The square gives IAIA, IAIO and IOIO outcomes, so children may be group A or group O, with a 25 percent chance for group O.

glossary.definition: Both alleles of the genotype leave their mark on the observable traits.
A marker molecule on a cell surface; blood antigens A and B are coded by the IA and IB alleles.
A grid diagram that pairs parental alleles to list every possible offspring genotype.
Carrying two different alleles for one gene.
